units.translation: 12 Etymologicum Genuinum (AB) αὐτόγυον after the words quoted at sch. 233/34b: "αὐτόγυον δέ: there are two kinds of ploughs. And the one is called πηκτόν, the other αὐτόγυον: the one that has its share-beam from a joining of timbers is called 〈πηκτόν〉; the one that has its share-beam from a single timber is called αὐτόγυον. The share-beam is a piece of wood into which the iron ploughshare is fitted and cleaves the earth. What the ploughman holds is called the handle. The small piece of wood passed through the share-beam, into which the handle is set, is the ἀλύη. The timber extending from this to the oxen is the γύης, and the part from the γύης to the yoke is the ἱστοβοεύς; and the parts of the yoke placed on the necks of the oxen some call ζεύγλαι, others βοεῖαι, others μέσσαβα. Thus I found a scholium on the Argonautica." cf. W 71 sch. AB K 353 Poll. I 252 Hesych. γύης. ἐχέτλη. πηκτὸν ἄροτρον Procl. Hes. Op. 423. Tzetz. ib. 427. 432
1 lacuna indicated by W, cf. Et. Gen.; after ἐντίθεται A, with the rest omitted, adds: "αὐτόγυον δέ ἐστι τὸ ἐξ ἑνὸς ξύλου κατεσκευασμένον"
b. αὐτόγυον: the distinction is with respect to the πηκτόν plough. Lg (P)
6 P adds at the end: "αὐτόγυον δέ ἐστιν, οὗτινος τὸ ἔλυμα οὐκ ἔστιν ἐκ συμβολῆς"

233-34a. He drove for Helios: the myth is fabricated on account of the god's lameness of feet. Yet it is not plausible; for he had greater power than the Giants, by which he would have routed them. Apollonius, however, has given the reason why Hephaestus made for Aeetes the bronze-hoofed bulls and the plough. That Hephaestus was powerful, Homer (Φ 342 sqq.) showed in the case of the river Xanthus.
10 ἐτρέψατο in L : κατεστρ- in P
b. Phlegraean: Phlegra is a plain of Thrace near Pallene, where the gods defeated the Giants.

14 Etymologicum Genuinum (A) αὐτόγυον: III 232-234. "Phlegra is a mountain of Thrace, where the gods joined battle against the Titans. It is so called because in it the Giants were consumed by the thunderbolt when they opposed Zeus." cf. W 71 Et. Gen. (B) Φλεγραία: "a mountain of Thrace. It is mentioned under the entry αὐτόγυον (where there is nothing in B)."
15 τ. Γ. κατεπ- in H : τ. Γ. ἐπ- in L : πρὸς τ. Γ. ἐπ- in P : 〈κατὰ〉 τ. Γ. ἐπ- Wil. ad l.
235. μέσαυλον: the middle of the courtyard, where the stalls of the oxen are. The Attic writers call μέσαυλον 〈the middle door〉 leading to both the men's quarters and the women's quarters.
16 sch. X P 112 Apoll. Lex. Hom. 111, 24 B. Συν. μέσαυλον (298, 16 Ba. Phot. Suid.) Et. M. 581, 6 Eust. 862, 14
17 supplied by W from a similar passage
237-38. And the ornate portico: there was a variegated colonnade on each side of the house. On the flank of the portico were higher buildings, that is, there were towers on each side.
